passage: Recess was only ten minutes today because of the assembly, and Akash was picking the kho-kho team fast. "You, you, you." He skipped right past Tsering, the new boy whose family had come from Darjeeling. "Not him, he talks funny." A few kids laughed. Aparna felt her face go hot. Tsering looked down at his shoes. There were only seven minutes left. Aparna could have just played. Instead she said loudly, "That's not fair. He runs faster than you, Akash. And how he talks has nothing to do with kho-kho." Akash rolled his eyes. "Fine, take him then." Aparna pulled Tsering onto her side. He tagged three people before the bell. On the way back in, he walked next to her.

qa.q: Where had Tsering's family come from?
qa.a: From Darjeeling.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when Akash said Tsering talks funny?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed for Tsering, her face going hot, because leaving him out was unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna face, and why did her choice matter?
qa.a: With only seven minutes left she could have just played, but she chose to speak up, which got Tsering into the game and showed fairness is for everyone.

qa.q: How might Tsering have felt when he walked back next to Aparna?
qa.a: Tsering probably felt relieved and welcome, after first looking down at his shoes when he was left out.

grounding: A child objects when a classmate from another community is left out of a game, showing fairness beyond her friends.

passage: Every evening the boys and girls of Sunrise Apartments played cricket in the parking lot. Bablu, whose family lived in the construction workers' sheds behind the building, watched from the wall. Today he asked, "Can I bat?" Arnab, who owned the bat, said, "This is only for building kids." Gopika, eleven, was fielding at point. She thought of her cousin who had moved to a new city and cried because no one let her play. She walked in. "Arnab, that's a rubbish rule. He's a kid. The lot is big enough." "My bat, my rule." "Then I'm not playing either." Two others dropped their gloves too. Arnab scowled, then held out the bat. Bablu hit the first ball over the gate.

qa.q: Where did the children play cricket every evening?
qa.a: In the parking lot of Sunrise Apartments.

qa.q: Why did Gopika think of her cousin when Bablu was refused?
qa.a: She remembered how hurt her cousin felt when left out in a new city, which made her feel strongly that Bablu deserved a turn too.

qa.q: Which choice changed Arnab's mind, and why did it work?
qa.a: Gopika refused to play unless Bablu could, and others followed, so Arnab saw the rule was unfair and not worth losing the game over.

qa.q: How might Bablu have felt watching from the wall each day?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and wishful, wanting to join but unsure if he was welcome, until today when he finally asked.

grounding: A child stands up for a boy from a different community who is excluded from a game, calling it unfair.

passage: "She can't play, she doesn't even understand Tamil," Manoj said, holding the ball. Dhruv looked at the girl standing by the school tap. Kiran had joined last week from Lucknow. "So? We can say the rules in English. Or show her." "It'll be slow." "It won't. Kiran, want to play?" Kiran nodded, cautious. Manoj crossed his arms. "Why do you care? She's not our friend." "Because it's not fair," Dhruv said. "She's in our class. If I went to Lucknow, I'd want someone to let me play." Manoj kicked at the dust. "Fine. But you explain." Dhruv held up two fingers. "Two bounces, then catch." Kiran grinned and caught the next throw clean.

qa.q: Where had Kiran joined from?
qa.a: From Lucknow.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv care about Kiran joining, even though she isn't his friend?
qa.a: He feels sympathy for her as a new student and believes it is unfair to leave her out, imagining how he would want to be treated in a new place.

qa.q: What choice made including Kiran work in practice?
qa.a: Dhruv explained the rules with simple gestures and words, so the game didn't slow down and Kiran could join in easily.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt when Manoj said she couldn't play?
qa.a: Kiran probably felt nervous and left out as a new student, which is why she nodded cautiously before grinning when she caught the ball.

grounding: A child insists that a new classmate from another state be included in the game because excluding her is unfair.

passage:
I'm Lalit, ten, the smallest boy in our colony's cricket gang. Last summer something happened in our colony that I still think about.
Santosh's family had just moved from another state, and at home they speak a different language. He sat on the wall every evening watching us play cricket. Nobody picked him. When he asked, one of the older boys said, "You're not from here. Go play with your own people." Some kids laughed.
My stomach felt twisted. Santosh wasn't even my friend yet. But it just wasn't fair. He lives here now, same as us.
I said, "That's not fair. He can bat after me." My voice shook a bit. The older boy rolled his eyes, but he let him.
Santosh hit a four on his first ball. After that, nobody said anything. Now he's on my team every evening.

qa.q: What did Santosh hit on his first ball?
qa.a: He hit a four.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he spoke up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was a little nervous, since his stomach twisted and his voice shook, but he still spoke.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the game, and what did Lalit's choice change?
qa.a: When Lalit said Santosh could bat after him, the older boy let him play, and Santosh became part of the team.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt sitting on the wall before Lalit spoke up?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and lonely, watching the game every evening in a new place where nobody picked him.

grounding: It shows a child who objects when a boy from another community is left out of a game, caring about fairness even for someone who is not yet his friend.

passage:
PE note, Tuesday. Jahnavi, games teacher, Class 5.
Mira joined us this term; her family runs the travelling fair and she will be with us for two months. In today's handball game, her team kept passing around her. When she called for the ball, one girl said, "She's only here for a bit, why bother?"
Tejas, who is on the other team and barely knows Mira, stopped playing and walked over to me. His ears were red. He said, "Ma'am, that's not fair. She's in our class too. Two months is still our class."
I blew the whistle and changed the rule: everyone must touch the ball before a goal counts. Mira scored the next goal.
Next: I will talk with the class about being fair to every classmate, and thank Tejas privately for speaking up.

qa.q: What rule did Jahnavi add to the game?
qa.a: Everyone must touch the ball before a goal counts.

qa.q: What does Tejas's red face suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous or upset but strongly that leaving Mira out was wrong, enough to stop playing and speak up.

qa.q: Which choice by Tejas made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Walking over to tell the teacher it was unfair, even though Mira isn't his friend, led to a rule change that included her.

qa.q: How might Mira have felt when her team kept passing around her?
qa.a: Mira probably felt left out and unwanted, as if being new and short-term meant she did not count.

grounding: It shows a child who objects when a classmate from another community is left out of the game, showing concern for fairness beyond his friends.
